meta.title: Who really said "Racism is still with us. But it is up to us to prepare our children for what they have to meet, and, hopefully, we shall overcome"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Rosa Parks, repeated everywhere, sourced by nobody. What the archives show about her most-quoted late statement.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Racism is still with us. But it is up to us to prepare our children for what they have to meet, and, hopefully, we shall overcome'?
meta.ogDescription: A late Rosa Parks line that circulates without a citation. We checked Wikiquote, Quote Investigator and her digitised papers — here is what turned up.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Parks wherever it appears, and it reads like her late public speech — she returned often to children, to preparation, and to the language of the movement. But we could not put it in a documented setting: no book, transcript or recording we could reach carries it, so it stands as attributed rather than confirmed.

source.heading: Where it comes from
source.excerpt: Racism is still with us. But it is up to us to prepare our children for what they have to meet, and, hopefully, we shall overcome.
trail: Not on Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks page. The Rosa Parks article ↗ carries a sourced list — her memoir, an NPR interview, the 1995 Washington speech, Quiet Strength — and this sentence is in none of it. It is not listed as disputed either. It is simply not there.
Quote Investigator has not traced it. A site search of quoteinvestigator.com ↗ returns no article on this wording, so the specialists have neither confirmed nor refuted it.

No match in her digitised papers. A full-text search of the Library of Congress’s Rosa Parks Papers returns nothing for the distinctive phrase “prepare our children” ↗. The collection includes her writings, notes and statements through 1998, which is the period this line is usually placed in.

An occasion is named online; we could not check it. Several reproductions place the remark in a late-1990s conversation with a newspaper columnist. We could not retrieve that column or any contemporaneous report of it, so we are not repeating the claim as established — a specific date and setting is exactly the kind of detail that hardens into fact through repetition alone.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced as it circulates. The closing phrase echoes the movement anthem We Shall Overcome, which is consistent with Parks’s late public speech but is not on its own evidence of origin.
source.rightsNote: We could not identify where this was first published, so there is no rights status to give, and it is definitely not public domain. Parks died in 2005; anything she said or wrote is in copyright to her estate, and if the wording comes from a newspaper or broadcast report then that publisher holds rights in the reporting. Credit her as shown, and get permission for commercial or published reuse.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.bio: Born Rosa Louise McCauley in Tuskegee, Alabama, Parks was a trained NAACP organiser and its Montgomery branch secretary long before 1 December 1955, when she refused to give up her bus seat and set the Montgomery bus boycott in motion. She spent the rest of her life — most of it in Detroit, where she worked for Congressman John Conyers — insisting that the moment was the result of organising, not of tired feet. She died in Detroit in 2005.

context.heading: The late Rosa Parks
lead: By the 1990s Parks was a living monument, and she used the position to say something more uncomfortable than the monument version allowed: that the thing she was famous for resisting had not gone away. Lines like this one belong to that late register — less the bus, more the unfinished work.

That is also why the sourcing matters. Sentiments attributed to a figure at this stage of public sainthood tend to get smoothed toward what audiences want to hear. This one is not smoothed — it opens by saying racism is still here — which is a point in favour of it being genuinely hers, and still not the same thing as a citation.
context.pull: Less the bus, more the unfinished work.
